profiles.meeting_scenario: At a university dental hospital, a troubleshooting meeting is being held after the quarterly quality audit showed that one endodontic service labeled 28% of root-filled teeth as 'failures' at one-year review, while the other services were between 8% and 11%. The discrepancy became noticeable after the hospital began using limited-field CBCT for selected follow-up cases and after restorative appointments were increasingly scheduled several weeks after obturation. The agenda is to diagnose why the same kinds of cases are being classified differently, identify the likely root causes of the discrepancy, and agree on an interim review protocol for chart audits and referral triage before the monthly morbidity conference. The expected outcome is a practical plan for re-reviewing the flagged cases and a shared-looking, but not fully shared, understanding of what should count as a persistent post-treatment problem.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: Nonsurgical root canal treatment, retreatment decision-making, post-treatment follow-up
members.background: Lena completed specialty training in endodontics and now supervises residents in a hospital referral clinic; she is known for conservative retreatment decisions and for emphasizing symptom-based clinical judgment in follow-up reviews.
members.private_state: She wants to stop the retreatment list from filling with teeth that are probably just slow to heal, keep the review protocol workable for busy clinicians, and avoid creating an audit rule that overcalls failure because of highly sensitive imaging.
hidden_assumptions: The clinically meaningful follow-up clock starts from the obturation date, because healing begins once the canal system is disinfected and sealed.
The proper baseline for judging healing is the immediate postoperative periapical radiograph taken after root filling, not an earlier diagnostic image.
In routine follow-up, persistent apical periodontitis should be judged primarily on serial periapical radiographs plus symptoms; CBCT is mainly for equivocal or surgical cases.
A useful root-cause review should concentrate first on tooth-level technical and restorative issues, because those are the factors the service can directly fix.

members.name: Dr. Vikram Shah
members.role: Oral and Maxillofacial Radiologist and Quality Audit Lead
members.expertise: Dental imaging interpretation, outcomes coding, clinic-wide audit standardization
members.background: Vikram trained in oral radiology and manages imaging quality and outcomes reporting for the hospital's dental services; he has published on CBCT detection of periapical disease and is focused on making chart review categories reproducible across sites.
members.private_state: He wants a coding rule that captures unresolved disease consistently across reviewers, avoids underestimating residual apical pathology, and builds a dataset that can support future work on systemic correlates of persistent lesions.
hidden_assumptions: The meaningful one-year review point should be anchored to when the definitive coronal restoration is placed, because that is when the final coronal seal and functional loading conditions are established.
The baseline image is the earliest diagnostic study that best shows the lesion extent, which is often the preoperative CBCT or pre-op film rather than the postoperative radiograph.

Persistent apical periodontitis is still present if a follow-up image shows residual periapical radiolucency beyond normal anatomy, even when the patient is asymptomatic; CBCT reveals the truer status.

A complete review of why a lesion persists should include systemic health and medication variables, because they may influence healing and may matter even if the tooth-level treatment was technically adequate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the 'one-year' or '12-month' follow-up as if it were a single obvious timepoint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 12 months after obturation of the root canal.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means 12 months after placement of the definitive coronal restoration.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each treats their anchor date as standard clinical common sense, and because both use the same phrase '12-month review,' the timing difference sounds already settled rather than something needing clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they will 'compare it to the baseline film/scan.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the immediate postoperative periapical radiograph taken after obturation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the preoperative diagnostic image that best captured lesion extent, often a limited-field CBCT.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In endodontic follow-up, 'baseline' is a routine shorthand and both have a legitimate default image in mind, so the phrase carries a false sense of precision without anyone specifying the actual study date or modality.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether a tooth still has 'persistent AP' or is 'still unresolved.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a clinically relevant persistent lesion: symptoms and/or no meaningful improvement on serial periapical films, especially if the radiolucency is unchanged or larger over time.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means any residual periapical radiolucency still visible beyond normal bone architecture on follow-up imaging, including asymptomatic cases and especially when seen on CBCT.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term sounds technical and shared, and both are using it sincerely within accepted professional language; because they are troubleshooting classification rather than openly debating disease ontology, the difference in meaning stays implicit.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in a 'risk factor review'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should 'review the risk factors' in the flagged cases.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes tooth-specific and procedural factors such as missed canals, fill length, coronal leakage, delayed permanent restoration, and procedural mishaps.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes those dental factors but also expects systemic health variables such as diabetes control, immunosuppression, bisphosphonate use, and other medical factors that may affect healing or broader risk interpretation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'risk factors' is broad enough to sound aligned, and in a troubleshooting meeting both dental and medical contributors seem naturally relevant, so neither notices that they are drawing different boundaries around the review.

turns.inner_thought: That 28% figure is far too high for a one-year review if we're judging these cases sensibly from the obturation date and from the immediate postoperative periapical. I do not want the retreatment list filling up with teeth that are simply healing slowly, especially now that a few CBCTs are picking up tiny residual changes. We need a workable explanation before this turns into a service-wide rule that clinicians can't live with.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The latest audit has one endodontic service marking 28% of root-filled teeth as failed at the one-year review, while the others are sitting around 8% to 11%. That's too big a gap to ignore, so I'd like us to work out where the classification drift has crept in and what we need to do before the morbidity conference.

turns.inner_thought: Most of the discrepancy is in asymptomatic molars, especially where the definitive restoration happened later and where follow-up CBCT was available. Before conference, we need everyone using the same one-year anchor, which to me is obviously tied to the definitive restoration because that reflects the final coronal seal and functional state. If we don't standardize that, the coding will stay noisy.
turns.utterance: I agree. When I looked through the outliers, the difference seemed to cluster in asymptomatic molars rather than the obvious symptomatic failures. I think before the conference we need to align what we mean by the 12-month review, because I suspect people are using the phrase as though it's self-evident when it may not be applied quite the same way across teams.

turns.inner_thought: For me these cases looked acceptable when you compare the review periapicals to the immediate postoperative film after root filling. A lot of them show some reduction or at least a trajectory that's not worrying, and without symptoms I'd call them slow healers rather than unresolved disease. I need to steer this away from overcalling failure on a single sensitive image.
turns.utterance: That's probably part of it. Quite a few of the teeth on that list looked acceptable when compared with the baseline film, and my impression is that a good number may simply be slow healers rather than true failures. If we're lumping all of those together, it's not surprising the numbers rise.

turns.inner_thought: When I compare the follow-up studies to the original diagnostic imaging, often the pre-op CBCT or the film that best showed lesion extent, several of those same teeth still have residual radiolucency beyond normal anatomy. To me that's persistent AP whether or not the patient feels fine. Symptoms are useful, but they shouldn't erase visible disease in the coding.
turns.utterance: Possibly, but when I compare the review images with the baseline film or scan, several of those same molars still show persistent AP even though the patients aren't reporting symptoms. From an audit point of view, that still looks unresolved rather than comfortably healed.

turns.inner_thought: At the one-year review, judged from treatment completion, I mainly care whether the lesion is meaningfully improving on serial periapicals and whether the patient has clinical signs such as tenderness, swelling, or a sinus. A small residual lucency on its own at twelve months does not automatically push me to retreatment or failure coding.
turns.utterance: In practice, at a one-year review, I mainly worry when the area isn't improving on serial follow-up or when there's tenderness, swelling, or a sinus tract. Those are the cases where I become concerned that we're dealing with a real post-treatment problem rather than a tooth that's just taking its time.

turns.inner_thought: For coding consistency, I've been placing any tooth with residual periapical radiolucency still visible on follow-up CBCT into the unresolved category. That's the only way to avoid undercounting persistent disease, especially now that we have better imaging. If we start requiring symptoms, we bias the dataset and miss the lesions I care about tracking.
turns.utterance: For the audit coding, I've been keeping cases in the unresolved bucket when there is still residual periapical radiolucency visible on follow-up, particularly on the cross-sectional imaging. Otherwise we risk undercounting persistent disease just because the patient feels fine and the note sounds reassuring.

turns.inner_thought: If we're going to review these flagged charts, the first pass should focus on things the service can actually fix: missed MB2s, short or poor fills, coronal leakage, delayed definitive restoration, perforations, instrument separation. That's where the practical learning is. I don't want the discussion diffused into everything under the sun.
turns.utterance: Then perhaps the useful next step is to go back through the flagged charts and review the risk factors in a structured way. I'd want to look at things like missed anatomy, fill quality, coronal leakage, and delays around the final restoration, just to see whether the pattern points to a technical cause rather than a classification issue alone.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and the review sheet needs to capture systemic variables too: diabetes control, immunosuppression, bisphosphonates, smoking, anything that may affect healing. If the treatment was technically fine but the lesion persists, I want that represented in the dataset. She'll surely consider that part of a proper risk factor review anyway.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. If we're reviewing the risk factors, I'd also like the sheet to capture the healing-related medical history in the same pass, so we don't miss variables that could be relevant when the local treatment looks acceptable. That would make the re-review much more useful from an audit standpoint.

turns.inner_thought: Fine. We'll recheck the one-year cases as I understand them, compare each to the postoperative baseline image I would normally use, and gather the practical tooth-level factors. That should let us separate genuine failures from delayed healing and stop an inflated failure rate from feeding straight into triage. If Vikram also wants extra background variables, that's harmless as long as the main clinical distinction remains sensible.
turns.utterance: All right. So the interim plan is that we recheck the one-year cases against the baseline image, review the risk factors, and then separate the genuinely concerning cases from those that are more likely delayed healing. If we do that consistently, we should be able to explain the discrepancy and avoid sending the wrong cases forward.

turns.inner_thought: I'll re-read the scans using the diagnostic baseline and keep the residual radiolucency cases in the persistent AP list, including asymptomatic ones. Then Lena and I can discuss which of those should matter for conference and triage. She seems aligned that the cases need another pass, which is the main thing for now.
turns.utterance: Good. I'll re-read the scans and pull together a clean list of the persistent AP cases, and I'll send that over before the conference so we can discuss the borderline ones together. That should give us something practical to work from rather than debating the headline number in the room.
